title: There's more to evolution than natural selection
subtitle: Life's complexity cannot be explained by random mutations alone
author: James A. Shapiro
introduction: Neo-Darwinian orthodoxy holds that life’s immense variety emerged through the action of natural selection on random genetic mutations. But, argues microbiologist James Shapiro, there is strong evidence that the mutations driving evolution are not random at all, but rather are the result of organisms modifying themselves. This upends the orthodox picture of life’s complexity as emerging out of simpler, lower-level physics, in a bottom-up direction. Instead, to understand complex living organisms we need to see biology as influencing the level of physics, in a top-down direction.
body:
Since the mid-20th century, the neo-Darwinian explanation of evolution has been scientific orthodoxy for the public: change comes from the gradual accumulation of random small mutations resulting from accidents in genome replication, and natural selection favors the survival of organisms with the “fittest” combination of mutations that permit them to reproduce more successfully than other members of their species. Given enough time and divergence, these gradual changes can add up to the formation of a new species. This is the story we find in popular accounts of evolution, like Richard Dawkins’ The Selfish Geneand Daniel Dennett’s Darwin’s Dangerous Idea.

Living organisms alter their own heredity. This scientific reality means that the time is long overdue for a radical revision of the neo-Darwinian orthodoxy about how and why evolution works.

There are serious statistical questions about the ability of random mutations plus gradual natural selection to produce the tremendous variety of genomic innovation observed in the evolutionary record. But the most curious feature of the neo-Darwinian account was the absence of any biological self-modification in the processes generating new organisms. Now that we can determine how hereditary variation arises by following mutational and evolutionary events with genetic analysis and DNA sequencing, it has become abundantly clear that biological cell functions, including those for DNA damage repair and genome restructuring, are the major (perhaps the only) significant sources of genome change in evolution. To be clear, this means that living organisms alter their own heredity. This scientific reality means that the time is long overdue for a radical revision of the neo-Darwinian orthodoxy about how and why evolution works. To illustrate why this revision is needed, I will focus on one of the most important examples of biological self-modification: the ability of cells to mobilize particular DNA sequences throughout the genome.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Life as we know it With Nick Lane

The story of biological genome change activities starts with a remarkable woman named Barbara McClintock. She pioneered maize cytogenetics before we knew about the DNA double helix (1953). Cytogenetics (literally “cell genetics”) was the science of correlating genetic changes with microscopic examination of the chromosomes in the cell nucleus. By the 1930s, McClintock could see that her maize cells recognized X-ray-induced breaks in their chromosomes and could join the broken ends together. When ends from two different breaks join, a novel chromosome structure forms. McClintock showed how structural changes can influence genome content, genome expression and chromosome behavior at cell division. These are all basic features of evolutionary change.

While mating maize plants she had selected to generate restructured chromosomes in the first cell divisions after fertilization, McClintock instead had a totally unexpected result. She had triggered “a genetic earthquake.” She observed greatly hindered reproduction: few of the kernels coming from that cross could grow into complete plants, and, in the plants that did grow, there was a new kind of genome instability that produced striped stalks and leaves and kernels with variegated expression of genetic markers. Years earlier, McClintock had observed a similar kind of instability with plants carrying circular chromosomes that were sometimes lost at cell division. But in doing genetic analysis of these phenotypically unstable plants, she found the source of variegation could sometimes move to affect a different genetic locus. She had discovered what we now call “transposable elements” that can move (transpose) to new genomic locations and modify the expression of nearby genetic loci. Focusing on the ability of these unexpected mobile genome components to alter the expression patterns of different loci encoding distinct characters, she named them “controlling elements.”

When McClintock first presented her experiments and interpretations at a genetics symposium in 1951, her colleagues were dumbstruck, and many were visibly outraged.

Nothing comparable was known to the geneticists of the day, for whom genes were fixed entities (unless some terrible accident occurred). We will see later how DNA sequencing analysis showed that McClintock’s appellation was prophetic. When McClintock first presented her experiments and interpretations at a genetics symposium in 1951, her colleagues were dumbstruck, and many were visibly outraged. The idea that genetic determinants could change their positions on the chromosome and modulate the expression of different loci flew in the face of scientific orthodoxy. [1]

My personal introduction to scientific research in 1964 was to begin studying the nature of hereditary changes (mutations) in E. coli bacteria affecting growth on the sugar galactose (gal- = bacteria that are unable to grow on galactose). [2] The majority of the gal- mutations I studied were induced by ultraviolet irradiation. In the 1950s, the Swiss physicist-turned-molecular biologist Jean Weigle had demonstrated that ultraviolet induces mutagenic activity, creating hereditary variation in E. coli. That activity worked even on viral DNA undamaged by ultraviolet irradiation. Like McClintock, Weigle provided evidence that living cells, this time bacteria, have an innate capacity to produce genetic change. Today, we know that the ultraviolet-induced activity was the result of a so-called “error-prone mutator DNA polymerase” that plays a role in the bacteria’s inducible system for repairing radiation damage.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Biology beyond genes With Denis Noble

My research on gal- mutations was not limited to ultraviolet-induced changes. I also studied spontaneous gal- mutations. I could determine the molecular nature of the DNA change in each gal- mutation by testing its response to different mutagenic chemicals for reversion of the Gal- phenotype to Gal+ (bacteria which do grow on galactose). The responses indicated that a significant fraction of the spontaneously arising mutations did not conform to the standard explanations for spontaneous DNA changes. [3] Moreover, some of these changes mapped in one DNA coding sequence had strong effects on expression of a protein encoded by a different sequence. I was eventually able to confirm that these strongly negative mutations were insertions of relatively long segments of DNA. A number of colleagues had isolated comparable insertions into other genetic loci. They could not have arisen by the kinds of accidents described in neo-Darwinian explanations.

Further study by a small coterie of laboratories revealed that the inserted DNAs were the transposable bacterial equivalents of McClintock’s maize “controlling elements.” They came to be called “insertion sequences.” Two of my colleagues and I organized the first meeting on DNA insertions in 1976 at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, where McClintock worked. We expected 25–50 colleagues at most would attend, and we were very surprised when more than 150 scientists registered. At the meeting, participants learned about antibiotic resistance sequences that used insertion sequences to transpose to mobile circular DNA molecules that transfer from one bacterial cell to another, a major factor in the rapid spread of treatment resistance. One of my co-organizers, Ahmed Bukhari, spoke about the mutagenic bacterial virus Mu that replicates its DNA by rapidly transposing to new sites throughout the E. coli genome, and there were talks about transposable elements in yeast. By the time I edited the first book on Mobile Genetic Elementsin 1983, there were chapters on maize controlling elements, insertion sequences and other transposable elements in bacteria, also in yeast and Drosophila fruit flies, mammalian retroviruses, and special recombination functions for genetic diversification in plants, mating-type change in yeast, and surface protein variation in pathogenic bacteria and protozoa. The path from accidental to biological mechanisms of genome change had become clearer.

Retroviruses are “retro” because they replicate their RNA genomes by reverse-transcribing them into DNA which they then insert into the host cell genome. To make additional copies, the inserted viral DNA is then transcribed into a new RNA molecule that is either incorporated into a viral particle or reverse-transcribed into DNA again and the process is repeated. Many organisms, from yeast to plants and animals, have elements that are structurally similar to an integrated retrovirus but lack any extracellular viral phase. Such a biological process is inconceivable to the neo-Darwinists, who envisage protein evolution occurring one amino acid at a time by random mutation. Transposable elements sometimes facilitate protein evolution by rearranging multi-amino acid segments with specific functions, known as “domains,” in a Lego-like fashion, to generate novel protein combinations. Such “domain swapping” also cannot be explained in terms of neo-Darwinian processes.

Transposable elements constitute only one aspect of the role living organisms play in driving their own evolution.

Three times in On the Origin of Species Darwin quoted Linnaeus’s dictum “Natura non facet saltus” (“Nature does not make jumps”). But this saying clearly does not apply to genomes because Nature has invented at least three mechanisms for organisms to make jumps in their DNA – the DNA transposons and retroviruses just discussed, as well as so-called LINE retrotransposons – and evolved many ways to determine the landing spots.

As we have learned from molecular genetics, cell biology and developmental biology, very few adaptive traits are encoded by a single genetic locus. Organic growth requires networks of coordinately regulated loci. How such networks evolve has been difficult to explain by neo-Darwinian mechanisms because each locus in the network would have to gradually evolve the proper regulatory DNA sequence independently, and the probability of that happening is vanishingly small. Transposable elements provide a straightforward solution to this evolutionary problem because any element can spread the same sequence to multiple locations in the genome, and there are mechanisms that can bias the insertions to appropriate target sites. Transposable-element rewiring of genomic networks has been detected in analyzing and comparing whole genome sequences from a variety of organisms. The adaptive traits encoded by transposable-element networks range from stress responses in maize to multiple aspects of reproduction in mammals to brain and nervous system development. Indeed, in a recent study, 63% of primate-specific regulatory regions were found to be located within transposable elements. In other words, were it not for transposable elements, we would never have evolved.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The agents of life With Johnjoe McFadden, Shini Somara, Denis Noble, Frances Ashcroft

I hope this brief review of some of the roles played by transposable elements in genome change has been successful in convincing the reader that biological self-modification processes are central to evolution. Transposable elements constitute only one aspect of the role living organisms play in driving their own evolution. Rather than accept the imaginary explanation that accidents and natural selection by themselves can account for all the complex hereditary variation seen among living organisms, the time has come to recognize the organic nature of the evolutionary transformations that life has used (and continues to use) to perpetuate itself.

[1] McClintock concluded that there exist two functional types of “chromatin” (as the genetic material was known pre-DNA from microscopy of stained chromosomes): (1) “genic” material that encodes the specific trait, and (2) mobile material that determines how the genic portion is expressed. It would take molecular biology another decade to arrive at the same conclusion, starting with the studies of Jacob and Monod on regulation of bacterial sugar utilization. McClintock was decades ahead of her time, and 32 years later, she received a Nobel prize.

[2] In bacterial genetics, DNA alterations are written in lower-case italics and corresponding cell phenotypes are written in plain text starting with an uppercase letter.**[3] These were polymerase incorporation errors (single nucleotide polymorphisms) or “frameshifts.” Frameshifts were accidental additions or deletions of one or two nucleotides that disrupted the three-nucleotide “reading frame” of the genetic code for sequential addition of amino acids to the encoded protein product.
